source.text: וְ/לֹֽא לָמַ֥דְתִּי חָכְמָ֑ה וְ/דַ֖עַת קְדֹשִׁ֣ים אֵדָֽע־׃

translation.text: And I have not learned wisdom, nor[a] do I know the knowledge of the Holy One[b].

footnotes.text: Or, “but I know the knowledge of the Holy One.” The Hebrew has no second negative; “nor” carries the first clause’s negative into the second, a possible Hebrew construction. The selected Rahlfs–Hanhart Greek makes both claims positive, including God teaching wisdom; the selected Weber–Gryson Latin makes both negative. These version readings do not settle the Hebrew clause’s polarity.
Or, “the knowledge of holy ones.” The Hebrew form is plural, but in Proverbs it can refer to God as “the Holy One.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect 1cs states the speaker's lack of acquired instruction. English present perfect ('have not learned') fits the confessional, present-result sense in context, though simple past is possible.
Standard rendering in Proverbs for practical and moral wisdom; no contextual reason to vary.
The noun commonly denotes knowledge. 'Understanding' is possible in some contexts, but 'knowledge' better matches the lexical pairing with ידע in the following verb.

Although morphologically plural, this form can function as an intensive/plural of majesty referring to God in wisdom literature (compare Prov 9:10). In this context, singular 'the Holy One' yields the most natural sense: knowledge belonging to or concerning God. The plural alternative is preserved in a footnote because the Hebrew form is genuinely ambiguous.

First-person imperfect of ידע. POB interprets the first clause’s explicit negative as also governing this parallel predicate, yielding “nor do I know”; Hebrew does not repeat the negative here. A positive contrasting interpretation remains possible and is disclosed in note[a]. The Greek and Latin edition controls differ in both-clause polarity and do not establish the intended Hebrew scope.

theological_decisions.issue: Whether קְדֹשִׁים refers to God singularly or to holy beings/persons plurally
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: singular reference to God: 'the Holy One'
theological_decisions.rationale: The plural form is syntactically and semantically ambiguous. In Proverbs, closely related language in 9:10 strongly supports a divine reference ('knowledge of the Holy One'). Rendering it singular preserves the likely wisdom-literature idiom without forcing a doctrinally loaded interpretation beyond the context. Because the Hebrew surface form is plural, the alternative is preserved in a footnote.
theological_decisions.doctrine_reference: Translation philosophy §3 (Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it)
